NeuroState-Bench: A Human-Calibrated Benchmark for Commitment Integrity in LLM Agent Profiles

Jia Xiao Affiliation: School of Artificial Intelligence Affiliation: The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen Email: xiaojia@link.cuhk.edu.cn
Abstract

Outcome-only evaluation under-specifies whether an evaluated agent profile preserves the commitments required to solve a multi-turn task coherently. NeuroState-Bench is a human-calibrated benchmark that operationalizes commitment integrity through benchmark-defined side-query probes rather than inferred hidden activations. The released inventory contains 144 deterministic tasks and 306 benchmark-defined side-query probes spanning eight cognitively motivated failure families, paired clean and distractor variants, and three difficulty bands. The main 32-profile evaluation contains a fixed 16-profile local subset and a matched 16-profile hosted large-model subset evaluated through the same benchmark pipeline. Human calibration uses the final merged reporting scope: 104 sampled task units, 216 raw annotations, and 108 adjudicated task rows, with weighted κ=0.977\kappa=0.977 and ICC⁡(2,1)=0.977\mathrm{ICC}(2,1)=0.977. Empirically, task success and commitment integrity diverge across this expanded grid: the success leader is not the integrity leader, 31 of 32 profiles change rank when integrity replaces task success, and integrity rankings are more stable under distractor perturbation. The primary confidence-free score HCCIS-CORE reaches 0.84690.8469 AUC and 0.69920.6992 PR-AUC for post-probe diagnostic discrimination of terminal task failure; the legacy full heuristic variant HCCIS-FULL reaches 0.79970.7997 AUC and 0.64100.6410 PR-AUC. Probe accuracy and state drift achieve slightly higher ROC-AUC (0.85870.8587) and better Brier/ECE, while HCCIS-CORE has substantially higher point-estimate PR-AUC and remains more closely tied to the benchmark’s intended construct. The exploratory neural-augmented variant HCCIS+N is weaker overall, and a randomized subspace control approaches chance. NeuroState-Bench therefore contributes a calibrated evaluation axis for exposing commitment failures over a broader model grid than the original local-only subset.

1 Introduction

Recent agent benchmarks have substantially improved the empirical study of tool use, web interaction, and long-horizon task completion, but they still overwhelmingly score agents by endpoint success [6, 26, 28, 25, 24, 29]. That emphasis is useful when the only research question is whether a task was eventually solved. It is inadequate when the research question concerns how reliably an agent preserves the commitments that make successful behavior interpretable, robust, and auditable. In multi-turn settings, an agent may momentarily overwrite the wrong state, bind the wrong entity to the right value, preserve the right value under the wrong provenance, or fail to repair a contradicted belief, while still landing on the correct final answer by accident or by later recovery. Endpoint success alone does not reveal whether those cases reflect genuinely consistent operational commitment integrity.

The present work addresses that gap by treating operational commitment integrity as an evaluation target in its own right. Importantly, this paper does not claim direct access to unobservable latent activations of deployed agents. Instead, it operationalizes commitment integrity as probeable commitment consistency between a task generator’s gold commitment structure and full-prompt-conditioned commitment elicitation through benchmark-defined side-query probes. In the current implementation, probes are asked as separate side queries formed from the full task prompt plus a probe prompt; probe responses are not appended back into the task attempt used for final-answer scoring, and probe-location metadata functions as benchmark metadata and downstream weighting context rather than runtime transcript truncation. Under this operationalization, the benchmark measures whether elicited commitments remain consistent with the constraints, bindings, trusted sources, updates, and repaired beliefs associated with each benchmark-defined side-query probe. This framing is deliberately conservative: it defines an inspectable, reproducible object of study rather than inferring mental states beyond what the implementation can support.

NeuroState-Bench contributes such a benchmark and calibrates it using human judgments of difficulty and construct validity. The released benchmark comprises eight task families, two variants, three difficulty bands, and deterministic instance generation, yielding 144 tasks and 306 side-query probes. A human calibration workflow contributes item-level difficulty, construct-validity status, and adjudicated annotation summaries. The benchmark is then used to evaluate the 32-profile grid used in the main paper, combining a fixed 16-profile local subset with a matched 16-profile hosted large-model subset over the same benchmark inventory. NeuroState-Bench is not a neural predictor of agent failure; it is a calibrated benchmark showing that endpoint success and elicited commitment consistency are empirically separable. The central empirical result is not that a neural-augmented score universally dominates simpler baselines. The repository’s own outputs do not support that claim, and this manuscript does not make it. The evidence instead supports a benchmark-validity claim: task success systematically under-specifies whether an agent’s full-prompt-conditioned elicited commitments remain consistent with the task-defined commitments required for coherent behavior, and integrity-aware evaluation materially changes rankings, stability analyses, and failure interpretation.

Formally, let 𝒯\mathcal{T} denote the released task set, let P⁡(t)P(t) denote the benchmark-defined side-query probes attached to task t∈𝒯t\in\mathcal{T}, let yt∈{0,1}y_{t}\in\{0,1\} denote terminal task success, let gt,pg_{t,p} denote the gold commitment associated with side-query probe p∈P⁡(t)p\in P(t), and let g^t,p\hat{g}_{t,p} denote the normalized full-prompt-conditioned elicited probe response. The benchmark does not attempt to infer unobserved hidden states directly. It instead evaluates a probeable commitment-consistency relation

𝒞(t,p)=[g^t,p=gt,p],\mathcal{C}(t,p)=\mathbf{1}\!\left[\hat{g}_{t,p}=g_{t,p}\right], (1)

where g^t,p\hat{g}_{t,p} is the agent’s normalized full-prompt-conditioned elicited response to side-query probe pp. Under this definition, outcome quality and operational commitment integrity are analytically distinct because

yt≢1|P⁡(t)|​∑p∈P⁡(t)𝒞⁡(t,p),y_{t}\not\equiv\frac{1}{|P(t)|}\sum_{p\in P(t)}\mathcal{C}(t,p), (2)

and the empirical purpose of NeuroState-Bench is precisely to measure how often these quantities diverge.

NeuroState-Bench is best understood as an evaluation resource and an accompanying analysis framework. Its core contributions are a cognitively structured task taxonomy, explicit side-query probe supervision for commitment assessment, a human-calibrated difficulty layer, ranking-validity analyses, phenotype discovery over agent families, and a carefully delimited treatment of auxiliary neural and mechanistic signals. The repository also contains HNCI, mechanistic-discovery, calibration, and BGIS modules. These remain scientifically useful, but in the current release they function as supporting calibration context and legacy comparators rather than as the central predictive claim.

2 Related Work

A first line of prior work evaluates agents through realistic task execution in external environments. WorkArena measures performance on knowledge-work tasks in a hosted enterprise platform [6]; OSWorld evaluates multimodal agents in open computer environments [26]; and τ\tau-bench studies tool-agent-user interaction in real-world domains [28]. These benchmarks have made agent evaluation more realistic and more operationally relevant. However, their dominant outcome variable remains task completion. They are therefore well suited to studying end-to-end competence, but less suited to isolating whether an agent can maintain benchmark-defined commitments under explicit side-query elicitation.

A second line of work examines memory and long-horizon behavior more directly. LongMemEval, MemBench, and AMA-Bench all foreground memory as a limiting factor in agentic systems [25, 24, 29]. Those benchmarks are highly relevant to the present paper, because operational commitment integrity necessarily includes memory retention and state updating. NeuroState-Bench differs in two ways. First, it is explicitly probe-supervised: each task carries benchmark-defined side-query probes that query commitment consistency rather than infer it only from final task behavior. Second, it frames errors in terms of cognitively interpretable failure families such as constraint persistence, binding interference, source monitoring, contradiction repair, provenance binding, and stale-state overwrite.

A third line of work seeks cognitively or neuropsychologically grounded evaluation. NeuroCognition and CheeseBench exemplify an emerging interest in benchmarking large models against structured cognitive paradigms rather than unconstrained task collections [9, 2]. NeuroState-Bench draws on this direction, but targets a different scientific object. It is not a general benchmark of cognitive ability in the abstract, nor a claim that LLM agents instantiate human cognition in a strong sense. Instead, it uses cognitive structure instrumentally: cognitive constructs guide task-family design, distractor families, probe roles, and human calibration. This makes the benchmark interpretable without requiring strong anthropomorphic assumptions.

Neural and mechanistic components are included as auxiliary analyses for constructing and validating conflict-sensitive evaluation signals; they are not intended to reframe the project as a brain-alignment or mechanistic-interpretability paper. The HNCI pipeline extracts conflict-sensitive human signals from multiple datasets; the mechanistic pipeline searches for agreement-related components in small language models and calibrates them against human-side targets; and BGIS applies a neural-orientation mapping to probe-level features. The released evidence does not justify a direct brain-to-agent scoring interpretation. The benchmark interpretation instead treats those modules as auxiliary analyses that help motivate calibration choices, document exploratory negative results, and bound what the current implementation can and cannot support.

Because the present contribution is a benchmark rather than a new agent algorithm, it also draws on methodological traditions outside the immediate agent-benchmark literature. The design and calibration logic is explicitly shaped by construct validity and measurement theory [4], inter-rater reliability analysis [3, 22], and calibration-aware predictive evaluation [1, 7, 8]. These references ground the benchmark’s measurement-theoretic claims. The central scientific question is whether the benchmark measures a coherent evaluation construct, not merely whether it yields another leaderboard.

Two additional literatures sharpen this positioning. First, newer agent benchmarks such as WebArena, AgentBench, GAIA, and SWE-bench push realism through browser environments, interactive tools, general-assistant tasks, and repository-level software engineering problems [30, 16, 19, 11]. These resources motivate the present work but still primarily answer outcome questions such as whether a task was completed or an issue was resolved. NeuroState-Bench instead targets the commitment-consistency structure that those outcome metrics leave unmeasured. Second, process-supervision and reasoning-faithfulness work highlights the scientific value of richer process variables [15, 17, 14]. NeuroState-Bench does not supervise chain-of-thought text, but it shares the same evaluation-science motivation: final outcome alone is often too coarse to support causal or diagnostic interpretation.

This concern also connects to benchmark-validity discussions beyond agent evaluation. Recent work on benchmark contamination and benchmark trustworthiness emphasizes that an evaluation can fail scientifically even when its reported numbers are internally consistent [27]. One failure mode is contamination; another is construct mismatch. NeuroState-Bench addresses the latter by making operational commitment integrity the measured object directly rather than assuming it can be read off from endpoint success.

3 NeuroState-Bench

NeuroState-Bench is generated deterministically by code rather than assembled as a hand-curated spreadsheet. The main task builder enumerates eight families, two variants (clean and distractor), three difficulty bands (easy, medium, hard), and three instances per family–variant–band cell, yielding 8×2×3×3=1448\times 2\times 3\times 3=144 tasks. Each task is assigned a family-specific cognitive construct, a deterministic seed, a gold state version, prompt metadata, and difficulty priors. The benchmark therefore exposes not only final prompts, but also the structured design variables from which they were produced. Table 1 summarizes the released task families.

At the inventory level, the benchmark structure can be written compactly as

|𝒯|=|ℱ​‖𝒱‖​𝒟|​ninst=8⋅2⋅3⋅3=144,|\mathcal{T}|=|\mathcal{F}|\,|\mathcal{V}|\,|\mathcal{D}|\,n_{\mathrm{inst}}=8\cdot 2\cdot 3\cdot 3=144, (3)

with |ℱ|=8|\mathcal{F}|=8 cognitive families, |𝒱|=2|\mathcal{V}|=2 prompt variants, |𝒟|=3|\mathcal{D}|=3 difficulty bands, and ninst=3n_{\mathrm{inst}}=3 deterministic instances per cell. Because constraint persistence emits three probes for each of its 18 tasks while the remaining 126 tasks emit two probes each, the total probe inventory is

|𝒫|=18⋅3+126⋅2=306.|\mathcal{P}|=18\cdot 3+126\cdot 2=306. (4)

These counts are not editorial summaries; they are consequences of the generator’s explicit combinatorial design and family-specific probe cardinalities.

Each task prompt is programmatically composed from a fixed contract: family name, cognitive construct, difficulty band, answer contract, scenario, initial instruction, context turns, distractor description, and final user query. The benchmark is therefore not merely a set of prompts, but an explicit commitment-tracking environment in text form. Difficulty is an explicit design variable rather than an after-the-fact annotation. The generator seeds each difficulty band with human-difficulty and integrity-weight priors, delay length, contradiction density, source-conflict count, near-miss count, and tool-noise level. Those priors are subsequently merged with adjudicated human calibration where available. Unsampled items retain design priors, which is why the benchmark can remain fully materialized even when human calibration covers only a subset.

The task-construction code makes this difficulty layer explicit. Let ωtdesign∈{0.85,1.00,1.15}\omega_{t}^{\mathrm{design}}\in\{0.85,1.00,1.15\} denote the design-time integrity weight associated with the easy, medium, and hard bands respectively, and let ht∈[0,1]h_{t}\in[0,1] denote the released human difficulty score after adjudicated overwrite where available. The merged item-level integrity weight used downstream is

ωt=clip⁡(ωtdesign​(0.85+0.30​ht), 0.50, 1.50).\omega_{t}=\operatorname{clip}\!\left(\omega_{t}^{\mathrm{design}}\left(0.85+0.30h_{t}\right),\,0.50,\,1.50\right). (5)

This definition is faithful to the calibration code and reflects an important design principle: human difficulty influences evaluation weight continuously rather than only through coarse band labels.

The benchmark’s key methodological choice is to treat operational commitment integrity as probeable commitment consistency under benchmark-defined side-query probes. Every task carries an explicit probe specification list covering the probe prompt, location, construct, role, gold state version, and validity status. The released benchmark contains 306 benchmark-defined side-query probes: the constraint-persistence family uses three probes per task to query early-constraint consistency more explicitly, whereas the other families use two. Probe scoring is family-aware. Responses are normalized and matched through the benchmark’s answer matcher rather than through naive string equality, which is necessary because some tasks require value-only outputs, some require state labels, and provenance-binding tasks require structured source-value pairs.

The released score family contains several closely related integrity scores. This manuscript adopts the confidence-free non-neural composition as its primary score and refers to it as HCCIS-CORE. It is not learned from held-out agent failures, and it is not a direct hidden-state readout. It is obtained by removing the confidence and uncertainty terms from the original non-neural heuristic and renormalizing the remaining non-confidence components, not by fitting weights to maximize terminal-failure AUC. Let dpd_{p} denote probe drift, let qp=1−cpq_{p}=1-c_{p} denote response-confidence risk, let upu_{p} denote the binary entropy of response confidence, let tpt_{p} denote trajectory risk, let xpx_{p} denote context-position risk, let sps_{p} denote success-probability risk, let rpr_{p} denote retrieval risk, let hph_{p} denote the human-difficulty signal inherited through the merged task weights, and let npn_{p} denote the auxiliary neural-conflict proxy clipped to [0,1][0,1]. The entropy term is the normalized binary entropy [21]

up=−cp​log2​cp−(1−cp)​log2⁡(1−cp),u_{p}=-c_{p}\log_{2}c_{p}-(1-c_{p})\log_{2}(1-c_{p}), (6)

and the context-position term is implemented as

xp=clip(0.45zp+0.35ϕp+0.20[vt=distractor],0,1),x_{p}=\operatorname{clip}\!\left(0.45z_{p}+0.35\phi_{p}+0.20\mathbf{1}\!\left[v_{t}=\mathrm{distractor}\right],0,1\right), (7)

where zp=posp/maxq∈P⁡(t)⁡posqz_{p}=\mathrm{pos}_{p}/\max_{q\in P(t)}\mathrm{pos}_{q} is the probe’s normalized position within task tt, ϕp∈{0.15,0.50,0.85}\phi_{p}\in\{0.15,0.50,0.85\} is the phase-risk schedule for initial, mid, and late probes, and vtv_{t} is the task variant.

The primary probe-level failure risk is

ρpcore=clip⁡(0.7059​dp+0.1471​tp+0.1471​xp, 0, 1),\rho^{\mathrm{core}}_{p}=\operatorname{clip}\!\left(0.7059d_{p}+0.1471t_{p}+0.1471x_{p},\,0,\,1\right), (8)

and the probe-level integrity score is ιpcore=1−ρpcore\iota^{\mathrm{core}}_{p}=1-\rho^{\mathrm{core}}_{p}. The older released full heuristic is retained as a legacy comparator, HCCIS-FULL,

ρpfull=clip⁡(0.48​dp+0.18​qp+0.14​up+0.10​tp+0.10​xp, 0, 1),\rho^{\mathrm{full}}_{p}=\operatorname{clip}\!\left(0.48d_{p}+0.18q_{p}+0.14u_{p}+0.10t_{p}+0.10x_{p},\,0,\,1\right), (9)

with integrity ιpfull=1−ρpfull\iota^{\mathrm{full}}_{p}=1-\rho^{\mathrm{full}}_{p}. The released tables retain separate primary-score and legacy-score columns for auditability. Human calibration enters the mainline score through the released item weights in Equation 5, the adjudicated validity weights, and the merged calibration tables rather than through an additional probe-level neural multiplier. Task-level integrity is then formed as a weighted aggregation of probe scores,

It=∑p∈P⁡(t)wp​ιp∑p∈P⁡(t)wp,wp=clip⁡(αp​ωt​νp, 0.10, 3.00),I_{t}=\frac{\sum_{p\in P(t)}w_{p}\iota_{p}}{\sum_{p\in P(t)}w_{p}},\qquad w_{p}=\operatorname{clip}\!\left(\alpha_{p}\omega_{t}\nu_{p},\,0.10,\,3.00\right), (10)

where ιp\iota_{p} denotes the integrity variant being aggregated, αp\alpha_{p} is the probe weight, ωt\omega_{t} is the item-level integrity weight from Equation 5, and νp\nu_{p} is the probe-validity weight. Because ωt\omega_{t} is shared by all probes within task tt, it cancels out of the task-level average whenever clipping is inactive; it becomes most important at the profile and dataset aggregation layers. For an agent profile aa, the released aggregation is

Ia=∑t∈𝒯Ωt​Ia,t∑t∈𝒯Ωt,Ωt=ωt,I_{a}=\frac{\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\Omega_{t}I_{a,t}}{\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\Omega_{t}},\qquad\Omega_{t}=\omega_{t}, (11)

and dataset-level summaries use the same item-weighted aggregation over evaluated profile–task rows. In the released configuration, the validity map uses weights 1.10 for adjudicated probes, 1.00 for probes validated during benchmark design, 0.95 for sampled probes, 0.90 for probes carrying only design-stage priors, and 0.75 for probes flagged as needing review. The release package also retains a neural-augmented exploratory variant, denoted here by HCCIS+N, with probe-level risk

bp\displaystyle b_{p} =0.42​dp+0.18​qp+0.12​up+0.10​tp+0.08​xp+0.06​sp+0.04​rp,\displaystyle=0.42d_{p}+0.18q_{p}+0.12u_{p}+0.10t_{p}+0.08x_{p}+0.06s_{p}+0.04r_{p}, (12)
ρ~p\displaystyle\tilde{\rho}_{p} =clip⁡(bp​(0.80+0.35​hp+0.15​np), 0, 1),\displaystyle=\operatorname{clip}\!\left(b_{p}(0.80+0.35h_{p}+0.15n_{p}),\,0,\,1\right),

and integrity ι~p=1−ρ~p\tilde{\iota}_{p}=1-\tilde{\rho}_{p}. The codebase further exports a randomized-subspace control obtained by shuffling released risk values. Across the released benchmark configurations used in this manuscript, BGIS is disabled as a mainline evaluation path and retained only as a legacy exploratory comparator.

This score family should be interpreted as a diagnostic tool aligned with the benchmark’s intended construct rather than as a purely ex ante forecast. In the release audit tables, state drift is a diagnostic post-probe variable because it depends on the gold probe label after answer matching; response-confidence and uncertainty risks are available immediately after the elicited probe response but are excluded from the primary HCCIS-CORE score; trajectory risk is available after the elicited probe response; and context-position risk depends only on benchmark metadata. By contrast, success-probability risk and retrieval risk are kept only in the exploratory comparator because they are more outcome-adjacent or optional diagnostic signals. This distinction becomes important in the diagnostic-discrimination section, where the paper explicitly avoids overstating HCCIS-CORE as a general-purpose optimized predictor.

4 Human Calibration and Auxiliary Neural Signals

The benchmark’s calibration layer is equally important to its scientific interpretation. The repository contains a stratified sampling workflow, raw annotation export, adjudication logic, and summary generation. The paper and Figure 1 intentionally report the final merged calibration reporting scope rather than the earlier 96-item calibration pass. That released merged scope contains 104 sampled task units, 216 raw annotations, and 108 adjudicated task rows. The dual count is intentional rather than contradictory: the merged sampled-item registry and the merged adjudicated scoring table are separate released tables after the final adjudication merge, and they therefore have slightly different row counts. The released merged-scope summary tables report weighted κ=0.97696\kappa=0.97696, ICC⁡(2,1)=0.97718\mathrm{ICC}(2,1)=0.97718, a mean absolute inter-annotator difficulty gap of 0.04810.0481, and perfect agreement in the released construct-label verification field. The benchmark also preserves scope-specific accounting for the initial calibration pass and the later focused recalibration pass, which is why the release distinguishes accounting tables from final merged calibration tables rather than collapsing everything into a single denominator. This is not bookkeeping trivia; it is part of the benchmark’s reproducibility contract.

Let ri,a∈{1,…,5}r_{i,a}\in\{1,\dots,5\} denote annotator aa’s difficulty rating for item ii, and let ci,a∈{0,1}c_{i,a}\in\{0,1\} denote the construct-validity verification label for the same item. The released normalized human difficulty score is produced by averaging ratings within item and dividing by the rating scale,

hi=clip⁡(15​|Ai|​∑a∈Airi,a, 0, 1),h_{i}=\operatorname{clip}\!\left(\frac{1}{5|A_{i}|}\sum_{a\in A_{i}}r_{i,a},\,0,\,1\right), (13)

where AiA_{i} is the set of annotators available for item ii. Pairwise consistency on a given reporting scope is then summarized by weighted Cohen’s κ\kappa [3] and ICC⁡(2,1)\mathrm{ICC}(2,1) [22]. This is methodologically important because the benchmark uses human judgments not merely for descriptive reporting, but to calibrate released difficulty and weighting fields. The release now adds an independent blinded construct-assignment check over 48 task–probe rows. Two annotators assigned each row to one of the eight benchmark families using only task and probe text, with task IDs, probe IDs, gold labels, and family/construct prompt headers hidden. Both annotators recovered the design family for all 48 rows, yielding per-annotator accuracy 1.000, macro accuracy 1.000, pairwise agreement 1.000, Cohen’s κ=1.000\kappa=1.000, and no disagreement rows. This does not by itself prove that the families exhaust all possible constructs, but it does show that the released task and probe texts carry the intended construct distinctions under label masking.

Human judgments behave in the direction required for a credible difficulty ladder. In the final merged calibration table, mean human difficulty is 0.44570.4457 for the easy band, 0.60860.6086 for the medium band, and 0.81180.8118 for the hard band, and the released summary tables record the monotonicity check as passed. Distractor items are also harder for annotators than clean items in the released calibration summaries. Construct-valid rates are 1.0 for both clean and distractor partitions in the released summaries, which means that the benchmark’s family labels are not merely design aspirations but survive manual verification in the released sample. Appendix Figure 5 visualizes the released calibration dashboard and makes the scope accounting explicit. Table 4 collects the most important inventory and calibration statistics.

The repository also contains a substantially richer human-side pipeline than the benchmark strictly requires. The HNCI workflow builds lexical, syntactic, surprisal, acoustic, and conflict regressors; runs ridge-style encoding models for fMRI; reuses temporal response modeling for ECoG; and exports event-, unit-, ROI-, and lag-level summaries. The current release materializes 218 event-level rows, 1,438 unit summaries, 14 ROI summaries, and 216 lag summaries across the Narratives, Podcast ECoG, and SMN4Lang resources. The control summaries show that these effects are present but small and heterogeneous: some fMRI ROI effects are on the order of 10−510^{-5} to 10−410^{-4}, one ECoG ROI family is negative, and a targeted temporal window in the Podcast ECoG resource shows a larger positive effect. These outputs demonstrate that the human-side resource layer is empirically instantiated, structured, and analyzable. They are not, in the current release, grounds for claiming a strong universal neural predictor of agent failure.

At the implementation level, the encoding analyses are regularized predictive models of the form

β^λ=arg⁡minβ⁡‖y−X​β‖22+λ​‖β‖22,\hat{\beta}_{\lambda}=\arg\min_{\beta}\|y-X\beta\|_{2}^{2}+\lambda\|\beta\|_{2}^{2}, (14)

with downstream evaluation summarized in held-out Δ​R2\Delta R^{2}-style statistics [10, 20, 5]. The current release therefore treats this pipeline as a quantitative auxiliary signal-generation layer with limited downstream utility, separate from the benchmark’s main result.

A similar caution applies to the mechanistic and calibration layers. The code searches for agreement-related component sets in GPT-2 and Pythia using predeclared campaigns, exports intervention-derived mechanistic features, and calibrates them to human-side targets using ridge regression with leave-one-group-out evaluation. Campaign selection is proxy-based rather than tuned on downstream benchmark outcomes; in the released run, both selected campaigns are sparse separator-based component sets. The resulting held-out incremental validity is small or negative. The released summary tables report a mechanistic mean Δ​R2\Delta R^{2} of −0.00197-0.00197, and the variance-partitioning tables show unique mechanistic contributions that are numerically tiny. In the notation of incremental predictive validity,

Δ​R2=R2​(Xbase,Xmech)−R2​(Xbase),\Delta R^{2}=R^{2}(X_{\mathrm{base}},X_{\mathrm{mech}})-R^{2}(X_{\mathrm{base}}), (15)

and the released results indicate that this increment is not reliably positive. This paper therefore treats the neural and mechanistic layers as auxiliary calibration context, not as central evidence for the benchmark’s value. This treatment follows directly from the released code and outputs.

5 Experimental Protocol

The implementation supports a broader serving interface than the original local benchmark core alone, including local execution and externally served large-model endpoints. The main 32-profile experiment therefore extends the older 16-profile local-only slice. This grid contains 32 profiles over the same 144-task benchmark inventory. The first half is a fixed local 16-profile subset obtained by crossing four base models—Qwen3-4B, Qwen2.5-1.5B, Falcon3-1B, and SmolLM2-1.7B—with react-style, context-engineered, planner-executor, and memory-retrieval wrappers. The second half is a matched hosted large-model subset obtained by crossing the react-style and memory-retrieval wrappers with GPT-4.1, GPT-5-Chat, Claude Sonnet 4.6, DeepSeek-Chat, Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct, Qwen3-32B, and Qwen3.5-27B. The benchmark therefore no longer rests its main claims on only the smaller local subset.

Both halves of the evaluated grid use the same deterministic task generator, the same probe specifications, the same answer matcher, and the same downstream scoring path. All runs in the main 32-profile experiment use deterministic decoding. The local subset is executed through the fixed local serving stack, while the larger-model half is executed through the repository’s OpenAI-compatible hosted path. This distinction matters for reproducibility engineering and compute accounting, but not for the benchmark’s measured construct, because the commitment-integrity computation is downstream of the shared task and probe outputs rather than specific to any single provider interface. The planner-executor wrapper continues to use the CLI adapter in the local subset, whereas the hosted profiles use OpenAI-compatible HTTP execution.

The fixed local 16-profile subset was executed on a single-machine setup with an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5070 Laptop GPU reporting 8,151 MiB VRAM, an AMD Ryzen 9 8945HX CPU with 16 physical cores and 32 logical processors, and approximately 31.8 GiB system memory. The exported hardware report shows four local server groups, all served with 4-bit loading. On this hardware, the 16-profile local subset required approximately one hour of wall-clock time. The additional 16 hosted profiles were executed through the same benchmark pipeline via a third-party OpenAI-compatible endpoint; provider-side accelerator configuration is not exposed by that endpoint. These details matter because the benchmark is intended to remain reproducible on commodity local hardware for its fixed local subset while also supporting a broader 32-profile evaluation for external-validity testing.

The evaluation pipeline materializes task-level and probe-level outputs, then computes benchmark-derived and auxiliary summaries. At the task level, the code exports task success, probe accuracy, state drift rate, repair precision, distractor susceptibility gap, the manuscript’s primary HCCIS-CORE score, the exploratory neural-augmented variant HCCIS+N, and a collection of baseline or proxy terms. Probe accuracy and state drift are complements of one another in the released implementation, so they provide equivalent ranking information but remain separately useful because one is a correctness view and the other is a risk view. Distractor susceptibility gap is computed as the difference between mean clean-condition integrity and mean distractor-condition integrity within a grouping. Post-probe diagnostic discrimination is evaluated against terminal task failure using AUC, PR-AUC, Brier score, and expected calibration error, with summaries exported overall, by family, by agent, and by agent-family slice. The code also supports bootstrap summaries and leave-agent-out reporting.

The current release goes further than ordinary bootstrap reporting. The reporting code now exports task-block bootstrap, agent-block bootstrap, and two-way cluster bootstrap intervals so that uncertainty reflects the dependence induced by shared tasks and shared agents. It also exports paired bootstrap deltas comparing HCCIS-CORE against HCCIS+N, probe accuracy, and state drift. Finally, it fits trained logistic and isotonic-calibrated baselines under leave-agent-out and leave-family-out protocols using the same benchmark-derived risk features. These analyses are not meant to prove that the hand-specified score is predictively optimal; their purpose is to test the stability of the benchmark’s qualitative conclusions and to make the auditability-versus-optimization trade-off explicit.

For a predictor producing task-level failure probabilities p^i\hat{p}_{i} against binary failure labels yi∈{0,1}y_{i}\in\{0,1\}, the two calibration-sensitive summary statistics used throughout the release are

Brier=1N​∑i=1N(p^i−yi)2,ECE=∑b=1B|Bb|N​|acc⁡(Bb)−conf⁡(Bb)|,\mathrm{Brier}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}(\hat{p}_{i}-y_{i})^{2},\qquad\mathrm{ECE}=\sum_{b=1}^{B}\frac{|B_{b}|}{N}\left|\mathrm{acc}(B_{b})-\mathrm{conf}(B_{b})\right|, (16)

where B=5B=5 bins in the default implementation, acc⁡(Bb)\mathrm{acc}(B_{b}) is empirical failure frequency inside bin bb, and conf⁡(Bb)\mathrm{conf}(B_{b}) is mean predicted failure probability in that bin [1, 8]. This matters for interpretation because the benchmark does not evaluate only discrimination; it also evaluates whether risk scores behave like calibrated early-warning signals.

Ranking validity is treated as a first-class analysis target rather than as a side effect. The ranking module computes pairwise ranking disagreement across predictors, bootstrap rank stability, leave-family-out robustness, leave-agent-out robustness, and a misorder audit that compares the released reference predictor (HCCIS-CORE) to task success. The misorder audit is not a synthetic summary only; it can be joined back to task prompts, final answers, gold answers, and, where available, raw traces. This design supports item-level auditability: when integrity-aware rankings differ from success-based rankings, the released audit can be traced back to task prompts, final answers, gold answers, and raw traces where available.

The ranking analyses can be written compactly. Let ψ\psi denote a scoring rule and let rankψ(v)⁡(a)\operatorname{rank}_{\psi}^{(v)}(a) denote the rank of agent aa under variant v∈{clean,distractor}v\in\{\mathrm{clean},\mathrm{distractor}\}. The release’s clean-versus-distractor instability score is

RIψ=1A​∑a=1A|rankψ(clean)⁡(a)−rankψ(distractor)⁡(a)|,\mathrm{RI}_{\psi}=\frac{1}{A}\sum_{a=1}^{A}\left|\operatorname{rank}_{\psi}^{(\mathrm{clean})}(a)-\operatorname{rank}_{\psi}^{(\mathrm{distractor})}(a)\right|, (17)

and the reference-versus-comparator mean absolute rank shift is

RSψ=1A​∑a=1A|rankHCCIS-CORE⁡(a)−rankψ⁡(a)|.\mathrm{RS}_{\psi}=\frac{1}{A}\sum_{a=1}^{A}\left|\operatorname{rank}_{\textsc{HCCIS-CORE}}(a)-\operatorname{rank}_{\psi}(a)\right|. (18)

The code also exports Spearman and Kendall rank correlations between these orderings [23, 13], which is why the ranking-validity discussion in the results section can distinguish between mere flips and globally reordered score geometry.

The phenotype analysis is equally explicit. The implementation first constructs a wide feature matrix by aggregating metrics over the family ×\times difficulty-band ×\times variant grid. In the expanded 32-profile experiment, the feature set includes task success, probe accuracy, state drift, HCCIS-CORE, and human difficulty over all 32 evaluated profiles. The matrix is standardized, projected with two-dimensional PCA, and clustered with KMeans using the released six-cluster configuration for the expanded grid. Stability is estimated by 25 bootstrap resamples and by leave-family-out coordinate shifts. Finally, case studies are selected automatically from benchmark outputs rather than hand-picked after inspection, with categories covering success-with-state-drift, baseline-missed warnings, and repair or distractor-overwrite failures.

Let MM denote the released metric set, and define agent aa’s feature vector as

xa=[μa,f,d,v(m)]m∈M,f∈ℱ,d∈𝒟,v∈𝒱,x_{a}=\left[\mu_{a,f,d,v}^{(m)}\right]_{m\in M,\,f\in\mathcal{F},\,d\in\mathcal{D},\,v\in\mathcal{V}}, (19)

where μa,f,d,v(m)\mu_{a,f,d,v}^{(m)} is the mean of metric mm over all tasks for agent aa in family ff, difficulty band dd, and variant vv. PCA is used only for the released two-dimensional coordinates [12]; KMeans is fit on the standardized full feature vectors by minimizing the within-cluster sum of squares [18],

min⁡∑a=1A{ℓa},{μk}⁡‖x~a−μℓa‖22,\min_{\{\ell_{a}\},\{\mu_{k}\}}\sum_{a=1}^{A}\left\|\widetilde{x}_{a}-\mu_{\ell_{a}}\right\|_{2}^{2}, (20)

where x~a\widetilde{x}_{a} is the standardized feature vector and ℓa∈{1,…,K}\ell_{a}\in\{1,\dots,K\} is the assigned cluster label. Bootstrap stability is then summarized through pairwise coassignment rates

sa​b=1B∑b=1B[ℓa(b)=ℓb(b)],s_{ab}=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\mathbf{1}\!\left[\ell_{a}^{(b)}=\ell_{b}^{(b)}\right], (21)

and leave-family-out robustness through per-agent coordinate shifts

Δa,f=|za,1−za,1(−f)|,\Delta_{a,f}=\left|z_{a,1}-z_{a,1}^{(-f)}\right|, (22)

where za,1z_{a,1} is the first released phenotype coordinate for agent aa and za,1(−f)z_{a,1}^{(-f)} is the same coordinate recomputed after holding out family ff.

6 Results

The first result is that the benchmark’s human calibration layer continues to behave like a valid difficulty scaffold after the evaluated grid is expanded. Difficulty rises monotonically from easy to medium to hard in the final merged calibration table, and the family-level performance tables show that agent behavior degrades most sharply in the families where commitment maintenance should be hardest. Constraint persistence is again the clearest example: across the 192 agent-task instances in each difficulty band of the 32-profile main experiment, task success falls from 0.44270.4427 in the easy band to 0.39060.3906 in the hard band, while mean HCCIS-CORE falls from 0.37100.3710 to 0.35200.3520. Delayed goal maintenance shows a similar but milder pattern, with hard-band HCCIS-CORE dropping to 0.57050.5705 from 0.60280.6028 in the easy band. By contrast, source-confusion provenance binding and stale-state overwrite remain comparatively strong across bands, with hard-band HCCIS-CORE values around 0.820.82–0.830.83. This pattern remains scientifically useful because it means the benchmark is not uniformly saturated even once substantially stronger hosted models are added.

Figure 2 makes this separation concrete at the family-by-difficulty level. The distractor penalty on integrity is not uniform across constructs. In the exported matrix, hard conflict resolution exhibits the largest positive distractor penalty (0.200.20), medium delayed-goal maintenance reaches 0.130.13, and easy constraint persistence reaches 0.140.14. By contrast, repair-after-contradiction shows near-zero or slightly negative distractor penalties (down to −0.05-0.05 in the medium band), indicating that its dominant failure mode in the current release is not simply distractor load but unsuccessful belief revision itself. Such construct-level variation would be lost in a single outcome-only aggregate.

The second result is that task success and commitment integrity remain strongly separable after the model grid is expanded. The task-success leader in the main 32-profile experiment is the Qwen3.5-27B memory profile (compact code Q3527-mem) at 0.93910.9391, but it is not the integrity leader. The highest HCCIS-CORE score belongs to the GPT-5-Chat react profile (compact code G5C-react) at 0.77720.7772, followed by the GPT-5-Chat memory profile (G5C-mem) at 0.77580.7758 and the GPT-4.1 react profile (G41-react) at 0.72770.7277. In the legacy HCCIS-FULL ordering, by contrast, the leading profiles remain the local Qwen3 variants. Relative to the primary HCCIS-CORE axis, 31 of 32 evaluated profiles change rank when task success is used instead, with mean absolute rank shift 6.81256.8125, maximum shift 2020, Spearman correlation 0.59750.5975, and Kendall correlation 0.41530.4153. These mismatches are not artifacts of a single family. The released agent-family breakdown shows that endpoint completion and elicited commitment consistency answer visibly different evaluative questions even when stronger hosted models improve both success and the primary core score.

A completed dual-annotator matcher audit over 193 stratified probe responses qualifies these estimates in an important way. The two annotators agreed on all 193 rows, all 97 automatic correct-match decisions were confirmed, but among 96 automatic incorrect-match decisions 45 were overturned as false negatives, meaning semantically correct answers rejected by the matcher, 36 were upheld as genuinely incorrect, and 15 were retained as unclear. Table 9 further shows that the unclear rows are concentrated in binding-heavy families, especially entity binding, whereas the false negatives are spread across several families rather than collapsing onto a single probe type. The reviewer package now also includes a completed balanced follow-up audit pairing 128 hard-case automatic incorrect-match rows with 128 matched-correct controls matched as tightly as possible on audit group, family, variant, and response style. All 128 controls were confirmed, and most hard-case rows were overturned as false negatives or retained as unclear rather than upheld as genuinely incorrect; Tables 12 and 13 report that completed follow-up audit separately rather than pooling it into the primary overall audit. The matcher audit shows conservative under-matching, especially for verbose hosted responses; the sensitivity analysis therefore treats the reported integrity estimates as stress-tested but not matcher-free. Table 11 bounds the primary-audit sensitivity directly: audit-row corrections keep the local-minus-hosted HCCIS-CORE difference negative (−0.0481-0.0481 to −0.0445-0.0445) and leave 30–31 profiles rank-shifted against task success. Absolute top-5 membership is matcher-sensitive in some correction scenarios, while the broader success–integrity separation remains.

The phenotype outputs sharpen this claim further. The exported behavior-space anchors in Appendix Figure 6 show that the point with the highest success rate is not the point with the highest probe accuracy, and the largest integrity marker belongs to the Qwen3 memory variant rather than the Qwen3 react variant. Since the clustering is computed on the full standardized feature matrix rather than on the two-dimensional visualization alone, this discrepancy reflects the underlying benchmark structure rather than a projection artifact.

The post-probe diagnostic-discrimination results reinforce a more careful interpretation. Table 5 shows that the manuscript’s primary HCCIS-CORE predictor reaches 0.84690.8469 AUC and 0.69920.6992 PR-AUC on terminal task failure in the expanded main experiment. Raw probe accuracy and state drift both reach slightly higher ROC-AUC (0.85870.8587), better Brier/ECE, and lower PR-AUC (0.59830.5983), while the repository’s simpler proxy baselines remain near 0.400.40 AUC and 0.150.15 PR-AUC. The randomized subspace control rises only to 0.51930.5193 AUC, which is still close to chance in substantive terms and far below the structured score family. The legacy HCCIS-FULL comparator reaches 0.79970.7997 AUC and 0.64100.6410 PR-AUC, and the exploratory neural-augmented comparator HCCIS+N reaches 0.77260.7726 AUC and 0.56930.5693 PR-AUC with worse Brier and ECE values than HCCIS-CORE. This result motivates the conservative interpretation below. In the expanded main experiment, the value of the mainline score comes from structured aggregation and human calibration, not from cross-provider confidence terms or a demonstrated gain contributed by the auxiliary neural term. The task-success predictor still attains an AUC of 1.0 only because it is an oracle upper bound defined by the target label; it is therefore not an informative early-warning signal and is not comparable to diagnostic predictors derived directly from the benchmark in a substantive sense.

The cluster-aware uncertainty summaries sharpen this interpretation. Under task-block bootstrap, HCCIS-CORE reaches 0.84810.8481 AUC with 95% interval [0.8111,0.8799][0.8111,0.8799] and 0.70230.7023 PR-AUC with interval [0.6182,0.7724][0.6182,0.7724]. Under the stricter two-way cluster bootstrap that simultaneously resamples tasks and agents, the same predictor reaches 0.84820.8482 AUC [0.7815,0.8923][0.7815,0.8923] and 0.70420.7042 PR-AUC [0.5916,0.7947][0.5916,0.7947]. The corresponding two-way cluster intervals for HCCIS+N are 0.77460.7746 AUC [0.6994,0.8361][0.6994,0.8361] and 0.57470.5747 PR-AUC [0.4484,0.6821][0.4484,0.6821]. These intervals support a more cautious interpretation than a simple point-estimate comparison: HCCIS-CORE is a strong diagnostic score aligned with the benchmark’s intended construct, but the evidence does not justify presenting its relationship to probe accuracy or to the neural term as a universal predictive-dominance result.

Paired clustered deltas against simpler comparators show a clearer pattern. Under two-way cluster bootstrap, the AUC delta between HCCIS-CORE and probe accuracy is slightly negative, at −0.0120-0.0120 with interval [−0.0258,0.0024][-0.0258,0.0024], and the corresponding delta versus state drift is −0.0120-0.0120 with interval [−0.0303,0.0022][-0.0303,0.0022]. In other words, the expanded experiment does not support claiming a raw ROC-AUC advantage for HCCIS-CORE. By contrast, the PR-AUC deltas are positive at roughly 0.100.10, and the comparison against the neural-augmented variant continues to favor HCCIS-CORE cleanly on AUC, PR-AUC, Brier, and ECE. Accordingly, the paper treats commitment-integrity scoring as answering a different evaluative question rather than as establishing a uniformly superior scalar predictor.

The predictor-gap outputs add a more precise interpretation. Relative to HCCIS-CORE, probe accuracy and state drift improve AUC slightly but lose about 0.100.10 PR-AUC and produce different calibration behavior. The legacy HCCIS-FULL variant is weaker than HCCIS-CORE on all four overall diagnostic metrics, the exploratory neural-augmented variant HCCIS+N is weaker on AUC, PR-AUC, Brier score, and ECE, and the simpler uncertainty, success-proxy, trajectory, and retrieval baselines remain far worse overall. In other words, the mainline score’s advantage is not a claim of dominating every scalar discrimination metric; it is a claim of interpretability, stronger precision-recall concentration than the direct correctness proxies, and ranking-validity evidence tied to the benchmark’s intended construct.

Figure 3 also clarifies why the random-subspace, legacy-full, and neural-augmentation controls matter. These controls test whether the score exceeds arbitrary perturbations while remaining interpretable when auxiliary components are added or removed. The exported diagnostics show this pattern. The random-subspace control falls to near chance, whereas the confidence-free non-neural HCCIS-CORE is stronger than the legacy full heuristic and the neural-augmented comparator in the released diagnostic-discrimination tables. This asymmetry is the main reason the present paper frames neural calibration as auxiliary rather than central.

The new sensitivity analyses show that this conclusion is not brittle with respect to the released HCCIS-CORE weights, but they also sharpen the right interpretation of “stable.” In the expanded grid, local ±10%\pm 10\%, local ±25%\pm 25\%, and Dirichlet perturbations do move some exact ranks relative to the released ordering. Under local-10%10\% perturbations, mean AUC is 0.84720.8472 with 5th and 95th percentiles 0.84650.8465 and 0.84830.8483, while mean absolute rank shift versus the released ordering is only 0.30600.3060. Under local-25%25\% perturbations, mean AUC is 0.84770.8477 with 5th and 95th percentiles 0.84430.8443 and 0.85230.8523, with mean absolute rank shift 0.86590.8659. Under Dirichlet resampling, mean AUC is 0.84850.8485 with 5th and 95th percentiles 0.84380.8438 and 0.85470.8547, with mean absolute rank shift 1.11871.1187. The corresponding mean numbers of profiles with any rank change are 8.48.4, 15.015.0, and 16.716.7. These perturbation-induced shifts are still small compared with the larger task-success-versus-HCCIS-CORE disagreement, whose mean absolute rank shift is 6.81256.8125.

The trained-baseline comparison adds a complementary perspective. Under leave-agent-out evaluation, the hand-specified HCCIS-CORE reaches 0.87370.8737 AUC and 0.76250.7625 PR-AUC, exceeding the trained logistic and isotonic baselines on both discrimination metrics while remaining worse calibrated in Brier and ECE. Under leave-family-out evaluation, the picture changes: HCCIS-CORE reaches 0.76480.7648 AUC and 0.59570.5957 PR-AUC, whereas the logistic audit-core baseline reaches 0.83810.8381 AUC and 0.54540.5454 PR-AUC. The intended interpretation is therefore not that the hand-specified score is universally predictive-optimal. It is that the released score is auditable, directly tied to the benchmark’s intended construct, and still competitive on the precision-recall axis most relevant to a sparse failure target.

The feature-availability audit further clarifies the proper interpretation of these results. State drift is a post-probe diagnostic variable that uses the gold probe label after answer matching; response-confidence risk and uncertainty risk are available immediately after the probe response but are excluded from HCCIS-CORE; context-position risk is determined entirely by benchmark metadata; and success-probability risk is deliberately excluded from the primary score because it is more outcome-adjacent. The paper therefore interprets terminal-task discrimination as evidence that commitment integrity is related to downstream failure, not as proof that the released score is a purely ex ante early-warning detector. The new confidence-comparability audit in Appendix Table 20 sharpens this caution further: the old full heuristic and per-agent confidence-normalized variants induce substantial rank movement relative to the primary HCCIS-CORE ordering. Confidence-related terms should therefore be read as legacy heuristic components rather than as universally comparable uncertainty measurements across local and gateway profiles.

Appendix Figure 9 provides a negative-control view that constrains interpretation. In the variance-partitioning exports, shared variance exceeds 0.650.65 in every reported row, while unique mechanistic contributions remain below 10−310^{-3} for GPT-2 and range from roughly 1.8×10−41.8\times 10^{-4} to 6.9×10−46.9\times 10^{-4} in four of the five reported Pythia control families. The one visibly larger Pythia baseline unique term in the primary-mechanism row reflects weaker mechanistic standalone fit rather than a positive mechanistic gain. As a result, the released controls support a constrained conclusion: the benchmark is strong evidence for a useful evaluation axis, but not yet for treating neural augmentation as a necessary part of the main score.

The ranking-validity analyses show why this difference matters. When agents are ranked by HCCIS-CORE instead of task success, 31 of 32 evaluated profiles change rank, with mean absolute rank shift 6.81256.8125, maximum shift 2020, Spearman correlation 0.59750.5975, and Kendall correlation 0.41530.4153. These are not uniformly small perturbations around the same ordering. Family-specific rank flips are even more revealing. In the constraint-persistence family, the mean absolute shift between integrity and task-success rankings is 6.68756.6875, with 31 of the 32 agents changing position. In the conflict-resolution family, the mean absolute shift is 8.71888.7188, with 30 of the 32 agents flipping. These families place trusted commitments under central task-defining interference, making endpoint success least reliable as a sufficient summary of agent quality.

The benchmark also reveals that integrity-based ordering is more stable under the benchmark’s clean-to-distractor perturbation than success-based ordering. The rank-instability summary reports a mean clean-versus-distractor rank shift of 4.34384.3438 for task success, compared with 2.75002.7500 for HCCIS-CORE, with probe accuracy and state drift also at 2.75002.7500. Appendix Figure 4 provides the full family-level instability heatmap; repair-after-contradiction reaches the largest family-specific clean-versus-distractor shifts for probe accuracy and state drift, while conflict resolution and stale-state overwrite show large success-based instability despite relatively modest integrity instability.

The large-model half of the evaluated grid preserves the same qualitative separation outside the older small local subset, but the primary HCCIS-CORE score changes the group-level interpretation relative to the legacy full heuristic. The hosted frontier subset attains slightly lower mean task success than the stronger hosted open-model subset (0.88910.8891 versus 0.90700.9070) but higher mean HCCIS-CORE (0.68800.6880 versus 0.65770.6577). Both hosted subsets are more successful than the local subset and also higher on primary HCCIS-CORE than the local subset mean of 0.62840.6284. By contrast, the legacy HCCIS-FULL score retains the earlier local-higher pattern because it includes confidence and uncertainty terms whose cross-provider comparability is limited. The benchmark claim is therefore not a fixed local-versus-hosted reversal; it is that endpoint success, elicited commitment consistency, and confidence-sensitive heuristic variants induce different evaluation geometries.

The phenotype analysis adds another layer of structure. In the expanded evaluated grid, the released PCA coordinates explain 23.25%23.25\% and 20.58%20.58\% of feature variance in the first two components, and the six-cluster configuration no longer collapses perfectly onto the original four local model families. The local families still occupy coherent regions, but the stronger hosted models partially co-cluster according to a shared high-success / moderate-integrity regime rather than by provider name alone. This is an informative result. It suggests that broad behavioral phenotype in the benchmark is shaped jointly by base-model family and cross-family scale effects once stronger hosted models are added. NeuroState-Bench therefore does more than rank agents on a single axis; it exposes reproducible performance profiles over failure families and model regimes. Appendix Figures 4, 6, 7, and 8 preserve the denser instability, phenotype, family-by-agent, and per-agent benchmark views that are kept out of the main-text figure set.

Finally, the automatically selected case studies demonstrate that the benchmark captures hidden failures that would be missed by endpoint scoring alone even in the expanded grid. One state-drift case study uses the DeepSeek-Chat react profile (compact code DCh-react) on a hard distractor constraint-persistence item. The final answer is scored correct (“Bay 14”), but probe accuracy is 0.00.0, state drift is 1.01.0, and the primary HCCIS-CORE score is only 0.11920.1192. A second case study uses the GPT-4.1 react profile (compact code G41-react) on a medium distractor constraint-persistence item; again the final answer is correct (“Packet D7”), yet probe accuracy is 0.00.0, state drift is 1.01.0, and HCCIS-CORE is only 0.11920.1192. These examples are selected from saved benchmark outputs under a fixed case-study rule rather than manually chosen after inspection. They provide concrete released instances in which endpoint success hides failed elicited commitments. Additional qualitative renderings are shown in Appendix Figure 10.

7 Discussion

NeuroState-Bench shows that commitment integrity is not interchangeable with endpoint success. It exposes cases where agents answer correctly despite state drift, reorders agent profiles, and yields more stable integrity rankings under distractor perturbation. The practical implication is that endpoint success should not be treated as a sufficient summary of agent reliability when commitments, provenance, constraints, or stale information matter. Reporting success together with HCCIS-CORE and probe-level summaries makes failures inspectable at the task and family levels rather than collapsed into aggregate error rates.

The benchmark is intended as a controlled diagnostic layer alongside broader capability evaluations. It can compare wrappers, model families, and serving interfaces under the same conflict-sensitive task inventory, and it gives benchmark users release materials for auditing whether ranking differences are associated with endpoint accuracy, probe consistency, state drift, or the confidence and uncertainty terms retained only in HCCIS-FULL. This is why HCCIS-CORE is the primary score: the released evidence supports a confidence-free benchmark score, while HCCIS-FULL, HCCIS+N, and the neural and mechanistic layers serve as auxiliary comparators, construct checks, and controls.

Its intended use remains bounded. Probes are side queries over the full prompt, so they measure elicited commitment consistency rather than hidden-state preservation. The 32-profile grid is not a model census; tasks are synthetic and deterministic; and the core score is engineered. The benchmark can expose hidden failures, but it is a diagnostic stress test rather than a deployment certificate or general safety guarantee. Public deterministic tasks may also invite benchmark gaming.

8 Conclusion

This paper presents NeuroState-Bench as a human-calibrated benchmark for commitment integrity in LLM agent profiles. The benchmark’s main contribution is methodological and evaluative rather than architectural: it provides a structured way to measure whether an agent’s elicited commitments remain consistent with task-defined commitments, not merely whether it reached the correct endpoint. The released evidence shows that this distinction matters empirically. Task success and integrity diverge, rankings reorder, perturbation stability changes, and automatically extracted case studies reveal hidden failures that endpoint metrics miss.

The released repository also identifies the current limits of the evidence. Auxiliary neural and mechanistic modules are implemented and scientifically useful, but they do not justify making the neural-augmented variant the benchmark’s primary score in the current release. This benchmark-first interpretation matches the implemented system and released results. Under that reading, NeuroState-Bench offers a concrete and reproducible contribution to evaluation science for agentic AI.

The release is also reproducibility-oriented in a way that is central to its value as an E&D submission. The release materials provide deterministic task generation, probe specifications, adjudicated calibration tables, task- and probe-level benchmark outputs, phenotype coordinates, rank-flip audits, and supplementary figure inventories. As a result, the benchmark can be inspected not only at the level of aggregate performance, but at the level of individual probes, tasks, and ranking reversals. That granularity is essential if operational commitment integrity is to become a scientifically useful evaluation target rather than an informal construct.

Appendix A Appendix: Supplementary Release Details

The main 32-profile experiment materializes 4,608 agent-task evaluations (32 agents over 144 tasks) and retains explicit benchmark metadata for benchmark generation, human calibration, ranking validity, phenotype analysis, and case-study extraction. The agent grid combines a fixed 16-profile local subset with a matched 16-profile hosted large-model subset executed through the same benchmark inventory and scoring path. The local half is factored into four base models and four wrappers, which is important for interpretation because wrapper-level differences should not be mistaken for differences between independently trained agent systems. The hosted half extends the grid with two wrappers over eight additional large-model profiles. The released summaries record this expanded evaluation as complete for the benchmark’s main E&D claims.

Table 6 summarizes this final expanded evaluated grid directly. The distinction that still matters is not whether the large-model half is “supplementary,” but that the local subset is fully local whereas the additional 16 large-model profiles are served through a third-party OpenAI-compatible endpoint. That distinction affects compute reporting and release packaging, but not the benchmark inventory against which all 32 profiles are compared.

Table 7 decodes the compact family-scaffold codes used in Figure 1 and the appendix per-agent views so readers can move directly between compact figure labels and profile descriptions.

The auxiliary release package is also substantial. On the human side, the HNCI release contains 218 event scores, 1,438 unit summaries, 14 ROI summaries, and 216 lag summaries, while the summaries record 12 SMN4Lang discovery subjects. On the mechanistic side, campaign search reports, selection tables, intervention outputs, feature tables, held-out calibration metrics, fitted mappings, and variance-partitioning tables are exported. These outputs matter because they document that the benchmark’s calibration context is materialized in released materials and analyses. Even where the downstream predictive gains are small or absent, the implementation is concrete enough to support careful negative or mixed-result interpretation.

The packaging of the release materials also reflects the benchmark-first interpretation adopted in the main text. The public dataset package includes the benchmark tables used for the paper’s 32-profile evaluation, adjudicated calibration outputs, schema documentation, benchmark card, validity statement, and paper figures and tables, while excluding raw traces and upstream human/neural source data. The anonymous reviewer package is broader: it additionally includes the annotation instructions, the rating-rubric protocol, and the anonymized raw dual-annotator rating matrix so that the reported weighted κ\kappa and ICC⁡(2,1)\mathrm{ICC}(2,1) values can be recomputed, the completed blinded construct-assignment packet with annotator files, summary, confusion matrix, and disagreement audit, the raw task/probe traces, the ranking-trace audit, the completed primary stratified matcher-audit packet with dual-annotator files, merged adjudication, and summary tables, the completed strict-schema side-query rerun over the primary matcher-audit rows, the completed balanced follow-up matcher audit with completed summary/adjudication outputs, and the supporting hard-case and matched-correct control component packets kept distinct from the primary overall audit. This split supports review-time reproducibility while keeping the public benchmark package scoped to the canonical release materials.

The release package also makes two conventions explicit. First, the earlier 96-item calibration pass is preserved separately from the final merged reporting scope used by the paper and Figure 1; exact table inventories are listed in the release inventories. Second, aggregate summary tables use an explicit pooled-row sentinel; this convention does not denote a 33rd evaluated profile.

The matcher-audit set can now be described more directly. The current release includes a completed primary dual-annotator audit over 193 stratified raw probe responses together with the two completed annotator files, the merged adjudication table, and a summary export. Row-level agreement in this audit set is 1.0. All 97 automatic correct-match decisions were confirmed, whereas the 96 automatic incorrect-match decisions split into 36 human-confirmed incorrect cases, 45 false negatives, meaning semantically correct answers rejected by the matcher, and 15 unclear cases. Table 8 further shows that clear-row matcher accuracy is lower on verbose outputs (0.64890.6489) than on concise outputs (0.85710.8571), and somewhat lower on hosted rows (0.72950.7295) than on the local subset (0.78570.7857). Table 9 adds the family-level split for those 96 automatic incorrect-match rows: the 15 unclear cases are concentrated in entity binding and source/provenance binding, whereas the overturned false negatives are distributed across constraint persistence, repair-after-contradiction, and source/provenance binding. A separate strict-schema side-query rerun over the same 193 primary-audit rows completed for all rows under the original-agent policy. It required a structured answer response and matched only the parsed answer. Table 10 reports a parse-valid rate of 0.9223 and a strict-schema match rate of 0.5078 overall; hosted rows parse cleanly in all cases, while local rows have lower JSON compliance. Because this audit set is stratified and enriched for automatic correct-match and incorrect-match audit rows, the strict-schema match rate should not be read as full-benchmark strict-schema accuracy. This rerun is reported as schema-feasibility and robustness evidence rather than as a replacement for the raw-output primary benchmark. The reviewer package also keeps a separate completed balanced follow-up audit rather than folding these rows into the primary overall audit. This reviewer-only follow-up audit pairs the 128 hard-case automatic incorrect-match rows from the second-round review set with 128 matched-correct controls sampled without overlap from the remaining probe inventory. All 128 controls were confirmed, whereas the hard-case rows split into 87 false negatives, 23 upheld incorrect cases, and 18 unclear cases. Table 12 summarizes the completed follow-up audit, and Table 13 breaks down the hard-case adjudications by family and response style. Control matching is exact on audit group, family, variant, and response style for 104 of the 128 controls, relaxes one level for 2 rows, and relaxes to family plus response style for the remaining 22. The completed primary audit therefore strengthens the release package where independent validation is most informative: it supports the existence of outcome-versus-integrity separation, while the strict-schema rerun and completed follow-up audit provide robustness checks without turning the release into a pooled overall-accuracy estimate.

These appendix figures support auditability because they preserve the bridge from aggregate summary to concrete release records. The main text argues that outcome-only evaluation hides commitment failure. The appendix then shows what those failures look like at the item level and how the released ablation family behaves under direct comparison. This division of labor is deliberate: the main body makes the benchmark-validity case, while the appendix preserves enough implementation detail for reproducibility and critical inspection.
